newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Fears of inflation, trade gap hammer Romania leu.
newsitem.headline: Fears of inflation, trade gap hammer Romania leu.

text.p: Romania's leu has fallen about nine percent so far this week, and traders expect the currency to suffer further losses, because of the expected worsening of the external trade position and fears of higher inflation. The leu has slipped to 4,700/800 to the dollar since Friday's close and traders expect it to slide below 5,000 this week as the local currency adjusts its purchasing power in relation to recent hikes in energy prices.
"I see the leu closing the week at 5,200/300," one dealer said. "This looks to be the level to which energy prices will be adjusted."
The interbank leu rate is still much stronger than the street value of 6,000 lev to the dollar at currency shops, which many see as a more realistic valuation.
The street rate has also been falling, and is currently nine percent down since the start of the year compared to a 15 percent fall in the interbank rate.
Traders ruled out a sharper slump on the interbank market in the coming days even though the longer-term outlook for the currency remained unclear.
The illiquid interbank market suffers from reluctance to sell by those holding hard currencies because of the unclear outlook for inflation and the trade balance.

The trade balance is feared to have deteriorated in the last two months of last year and the International Monetary Fund estimates the final trade gap for 1996 was close to $2 billion, boosted by purchases of fuel needed to cope with a harsh winter.

Inflation is feared to have risen after the new reformist government, in power since the defeat of ex-communists in last November's elections, doubled petrol prices from January, aligning them to world levels.
"The recent price hikes have also undermined confidence in the leu," one trader said.

The leu's downward move began to gather pace after the new cabinet took office last December. So far the central bank, whose hard currency reserves were an estimated $855.2 million at end-1996, has refrained from intervening to halt the leu's fall.
Electricity and heating prices are also expected to go up this week, with economists predicting a quickening of inflation to over 10 percent monthly in January, up from November's 5.8.
Year-on-year inflation stood at 47.4 percent last November, well above an initial target of 20 percent.

In a bid to tighten money supply and prevent a rise in inflation the central bank (BNR) raised the discount rate to 50 percent from 35 percent starting in January. Its auctioned credit rate jumped last week to 59.23 from 53 percent.
